newsitem.title: CANADA: Lower chemical returns cut NOVA Q3 profit.
newsitem.headline: Lower chemical returns cut NOVA Q3 profit.

text.p: Canadian pipeline and petrochemical firm NOVA Corp said on Tuesday that lower prices and higher costs in its chemical division resulted in lower third-quarter earnings.
NOVA reported third-quarter earnings of C$123 million or C$0.26 a share, down from C$155 million or C$0.31 per share in the year earlier period.
Operating income at NOVA Chemicals fell to C$68 million in the third quarter from C$102 million last year.
The company said the decrease from last year was due to lower styrene prices and higher crude oil feedstock costs.
The average U.S. Gulf Coast styrene price in the quarter fell to US$0.32 a pound from US$0.49 in the third quarter of 1995. Prices have stayed near current levels for all of 1996.
The company also realized lower prices than last year for polystyrene and propylene.
But prices for linear low-density polyethylene climbed since last year to US$0.45 a pound from US$0.35 in the fourth quarter of 1995.
The company said higher chemical sales volumes in the quarter helped offset the general weakness in prices.
"Polyethylene sales volumes were strong throughout the quarter, up 6 percent compared to the second quarter, and up 18 percent compared to the third quarter of 1995," NOVA said.
Unit NOVA Gas Transmission made a C$42 million contribution to the company's earnings in the third quarter, unchanged from last year.
NGTL, which faces increasing pressure from companies aiming to build natural gas pipelines that would cut across its Alberta turf, said it planned to protect its interests.

Current by-pass pipeline proposals include the producer-backed Alliance project to Chicago from northeast British Columbia and the PanCanadian Petroleum -Westcoast Energy Palliser project in southern Alberta.

"NOVA opposes these by-pass proposals on the grounds they are not in the public interest," it said. "Duplication of existing systems might offer lower prices for a few proponents, but would lead to overall higher transportation costs and tolls for most producers."
